conditions.name: Hemlock woolly adelgid
symptoms: White, cottony egg sacs at needle bases on twig undersides (diagnostic)
Needles turn gray-green and drop
Twig death progressing from the bottom up
biology: White woolly masses at the base of needles on the underside of twigs. Spring crawlers Apr–May. A summer dormant stage lasts until cooler fall weather. Nymphs develop through winter, adults appear in late winter, and egg-laying females are present late Mar–early Apr. Flupyradifurone used for other pests may also suppress HWA.

Update (Oct 2026): Michigan State guidance: dinotefuran moves fast and is best on heavily infested or declining trees, but lasts only 1–2 years. Imidacloprid takes a year or more to reach the top of large trees but protects for 4–7 years. For heavily infested trees, applicators use a basal bark tank mix of both for rapid knockdown plus long-term protection. Check both labels allow basal bark use and tank mixing (FIFRA 2(ee)). Judge dinotefuran by new growth the following late fall or winter, and imidacloprid a year after treatment.

Update (Oct 2026): Virginia, Maryland and federal programs release predator beetles (Laricobius nigrinus) and silver flies (Leucotaraxis) for long-term HWA control. Coordinate with the state forest health program before treating trees at or near release sites.

Update (Oct 2026): Current NC State and UGA guidance for granulate ambrosia beetle: protect high-value, young or stressed trees with pyrethroid trunk sprays re-applied every 2–3 weeks through the spring flight. Highly susceptible hosts include dogwood, redbud, maples, flowering cherry, crape myrtle, magnolia, styrax, sweetgum and azalea.

conditions.name: Oak wilt
biology: Wilting and browning of leaves, rapid defoliation and branch dieback. Live oaks may show yellowing along leaf veins. The red oak group is highly susceptible, and diseased red oaks will not recover. White oaks are resistant and may recover with treatment. Red and white oaks do not root-graft with each other.

Update (Oct 2026): Sap beetles find fresh wounds within minutes, and wounds stay attractive for about 3 days. If an oak must be pruned or wounded during the growing season, seal the wound immediately. This is the one case where wound paint is recommended. Do not move unseasoned firewood from diseased red oaks. Repeat preventive propiconazole about every 2 years.

conditions.name: Rose rosette
biology: A virus affecting most roses, including Knock Out and multiflora rose. Spread by eriophyid mites and likely through root grafts. Causes stunting and witches' brooms. Affected plants decline and die.

Update (Oct 2026): Current extension guidance (UGA 2025, Colorado State 2025, UT 2024) is to remove symptomatic plants early, roots included, bagged and not composted. Miticides are not recommended or have shown limited effect. In the 2018 Texas A&M / Tennessee field trial, roses sprayed every 14 days with fenpyroximate, spiromesifen, spirotetramat or bifenthrin stayed symptom-free, while **abamectin + oil was ineffective**. If a miticide program is sold to protect nearby high-value roses, use those products and present it as unproven.

conditions.name: Tree growth regulation (paclobutrazol)
biology: Paclobutrazol reduces twig elongation for 2–4 years. Candidates are trees that have outgrown their site or will soon: trees under wires, by windows or signs, vista trees, parking lot trees and others that need frequent pruning. Treated trees lose less water in drought, which helps non-irrigated trees and trees with bacterial leaf scorch or Verticillium wilt. Declining trees with limited rooting area may be treated to reduce decline symptoms. If root space is not limited (radius over 3× DBH), root invigoration is preferred. Expect about a one-season lag before any effect.

treatments.title: Do not treat trees with severe trunk injury or significant girdling roots. Wait if soil is saturated.
Where the tree had root invigoration, delay growth-regulator treatment at least one growing season.

conditions.name: Japanese knotweed
biology: Extremely invasive and needs multiple treatments. Live plant parts removed from the site can root and invade the disposal site.

Update (Oct 2026): Late-season timing is what kills the rhizomes. After flowering (September–October), knotweed sends sugars to its roots and carries herbicide with them. If cut, wait at least 8 weeks before spraying regrowth. Results may not show until the next spring.

conditions.name: Bamboo
biology: Running bamboo spreads aggressively. Suppression takes repeated treatments over several years.

conditions.name: Phragmites

conditions.name: Deer browse
biology: Repellents work best under low to moderate deer pressure with other food available. For high-value plants where no damage can be tolerated, use fences, barriers or netting. Rotate repellents so deer do not get used to one product.

treatments.title: Tall fences exclude deer. Use netting or cages on high-value plants.
Deer repellent (putrescent egg + capsaicin) (foliar spray)

conditions.name: Sapsucker
biology: Sapsuckers are protected migratory woodpeckers that drill rows of holes in stems and scaffold branches. They tend to feed on trees with previous damage. They spend summer in the North and winter in the South.

treatments.title: Wrap damaged stems with burlap or roof-repair fabric before feeding starts. Remove the wrap when sapsuckers migrate.

warnings: No effective chemical treatment: Sapsuckers are protected.

conditions.name: Slugs and snails
biology: Mollusks that need shaded, damp sites during the day.

treatments.title: Remove debris such as logs and flat stones. Remove mulch if feasible, and competing weeds.
Prune overstory plants to improve light and air.
Iron phosphate bait (granular / bait)

schedule.window: Broadcast near susceptible plants. Wet dry soil first. Repeat about every 14 d except in very wet weather

notes: Pet and wildlife safe

conditions.name: Voles
biology: Also called meadow mice. They chew bark and wood at the root collar and low stem, mostly in the dormant season, and feed on perennials in summer. Dense plantings such as juniper beds are most susceptible. Voles run tunnels at the soil–mulch interface.

treatments.title: Put an expanded slate band around the root collar, about 1 inch deep under the mulch, and several inches below the soil surface where possible.

conditions.name: Apple fruit program
biology: A basic spray program for home apples (6 visits). New clients may need 8–12 inspections in year 1, dropping to 5–6 by year 2–3. Use 6–12 treatments where special issues like fire blight exist. Extra monthly cover sprays can follow the third cover where codling moth and mildew pressure is severe. For codling moth IPM, use pheromone disruption ties with Trichogramma wasps.

treatments.title: Prune annually for light and air. Remove dead and diseased wood.
Pick up dropped fruit. Remove mummies.
Fertilize based on a soil test. Phosphite soil applications may improve root health where root disease is a concern.
Pheromone mating-disruption ties for codling moth.

notes: Low rate. Only highly susceptible varieties

conditions.name: Pear fruit program
biology: A basic spray program for home pears (6 visits). Myclobutanil is not registered on pear. Use permethrin only in the dormant and delayed-dormant periods, where it is optimal for pear psylla.

biology: A basic spray program for home peaches, cherries, apricots, nectarines and plums (6 visits). Brown rot becomes severe as fruit ripens, so consider extra sprays during ripening. Pheromone traps for oriental fruit moth and lesser peachtree borer help time applications.

Remove fruit mummies and dropped fruit.

Host choice matters: P. phillyreifolia and P. japonica 'Variegata' resisted lace bugs in trials, while 'Cavatine' and 'Temple Bells' were susceptible.

treatments.title: Plant Pieris in part shade. Sun-exposed plants are damaged most.
Use resistant Pieris (P. phillyreifolia, P. japonica 'Variegata') for new plantings.

biology: A white, waxy aphid on hackberry leaf undersides (Shivaphis celti). It drips heavy honeydew and causes sooty mold over cars, patios and paving. Trees are not seriously harmed. conditions.name: Filbert big bud mite
biology: Eriophyid mites (Phytoptus avellanae and Cecidophyopsis vermiformis) live inside hazelnut buds, which swell abnormally ("big bud") and often die. Inside the galls, mites are protected from sprays, so treatments must hit mites as they move to new buds in spring before galls form. Cultivars differ in susceptibility.

conditions.name: Cypress twig gall midge
biology: Midges lay eggs on new bald cypress growth in late spring, and larvae induce spongy twig galls that turn brown and weigh branches down. Damage is mostly cosmetic. Insecticides are not advised because natural enemies emerging with the midges usually regulate populations.

treatments.title: Rake up and destroy fallen galls in autumn or early spring, before the midges emerge.

conditions.name: Hackberry witches' broom
biology: Dense clusters of short twigs on hackberry, linked to an eriophyid mite and a powdery mildew fungus. Cosmetic, with no lasting harm to tree health.

treatments.title: Prune out brooms where they are unsightly or create dense, weak branching.

conditions.name: Larch casebearer
biology: Tiny caterpillars living in cigar-shaped cases mine new larch needles in spring. Heavy populations make trees look bronzed by mid-June. Adults fly late June to early July. Introduced parasitoids and weather usually regulate populations, and extension sources list no routine landscape spray.

treatments.title: Scout new foliage as it emerges in spring for mined, whitened needles and cases.
Avoid planting larch in open-grown edge sites, which are attacked most.
Water and mulch heavily defoliated trees to support refoliation.

conditions.name: Elm zigzag sawfly
biology: Invasive sawfly first found in North America in Virginia (2021), now in Maryland and neighboring states. Larvae feed in a zigzag pattern from the leaf edge inward, then consume whole leaves. Several generations a year can defoliate elms by late summer. Healthy elms usually recover from occasional defoliation, so treatment is rarely needed except on high-value or stressed trees. No insecticide is labeled specifically for it yet. Use products labeled for sawflies on trees and shrubs.

treatments.title: Look for zigzag feeding on elm leaves from May. Report new county finds to the state department of agriculture.
On small trees, pick larvae off into soapy water.
Water and mulch defoliated elms to support recovery.
Spinosad (foliar spray)

schedule.window: As soon as larvae are found feeding in spring, repeat for later generations

notes: Use a product labeled for sawflies on trees

notes: Pyrethroid mite-flare risk

treatments.title: Dinotefuran (foliar spray)

conditions.name: Beech leaf disease
biology: Caused by a foliar nematode (Litylenchus crenatae mccannii). Current best practice for high-value trees is thiabendazole root flare injection every 2–3 years, with phosphite basal bark or soil applications and foliar fluopyram as alternatives or additions. Dark green bands between the leaf veins, seen best from below, then thickened, leathery, crinkled leaves, bud abortion, thinning canopy and death of smaller trees within years. Nematodes overwinter in buds and move into new buds from late summer. Confirmed in Prince William County, VA (2021), spreading in Northern Virginia, and confirmed in at least 12 Maryland counties plus Baltimore City (MDA, 2025). There is no cure. Treatments suppress symptoms on individual high-value trees. Trees in dense beech stands are poor candidates for foliar treatment because untreated neighbors reinfest them.

treatments.title: Look for dark interveinal banding on leaves (seen best from below) and aborted buds. Report new finds to the state forest health program.
Mulch the root zone and irrigate in drought to reduce stress.
A summer root biostimulant may help offset stress. Avoid excess nitrogen.
In dense stands, plan for loss of heavily affected trees. Remove hazardous dead beech.
Thiabendazole (macro-injection)

schedule.window: Root flare injection at or below ground level, after leaf expansion with moist soil

notes: Peer-reviewed (Loyd et al. 2025, Arboriculture & Urban Forestry): improved canopy and reduced nematodes in buds at 11 and 22 months. Labeled for BLD (Arbotect 20-S). Fairfax County rates it "very effective". Trunk-wood injection is less effective. Retreat every 2–3+ years or when symptoms return

treatments.title: Potassium phosphite (basal bark)

notes: Published protocols use 2 applications a month apart. A third is arborist practice. CAES: a surfactant (e.g. Pentra-Bark) does not improve uptake. Results build over several years

notes: Peer-reviewed suppression (Bartlett/USDA-ARS 2025). Best on isolated trees. Very toxic to aquatic life: no use near water or storm drains. Professional use. Rotate modes of action

conditions.name: Boxwood dieback
biology: Caused by the fungus Colletotrichum theobromicola. Leaves bleach to tan, often on scattered branches, with dark streaks under the bark of affected stems. It spreads on infected nursery stock and may enter through pruning cuts. Do not confuse it with boxwood blight (black stem lesions, rapid leaf drop) or Volutella blight. Phytophthora root rot programs do not control it. No preventive spray is recommended by Virginia Cooperative Extension. Lab tests rank difenoconazole + pydiflumetofen and the strobilurin mixes highest, but these are not field-validated.

treatments.title: Remove and destroy symptomatic plants. Pruning out dead twigs does not control it.
Disinfect pruning tools between plants. Avoid unnecessary wounding and pruning in wet weather.
Inspect and isolate new boxwood. Buy from nurseries with clean-stock programs.
Send samples to a diagnostic lab to separate dieback from blight and Volutella.

conditions.name: Tree of heaven control
biology: An invasive tree and the preferred host of spotted lanternfly. Cutting it without herbicide makes it worse, because it answers with masses of stump sprouts and root suckers, and cut-stump treatment also encourages suckering. Use hack-and-squirt in mid to late summer so herbicide moves to the roots. Expect follow-up treatment of resprouts for several years. Where lanternfly is present, keep a few male trees as systemic-treated trap trees (see Spotted lanternfly).

treatments.title: Do not cut tree of heaven before herbicide. For hazard trees, treat first and fell about 30 days later.
Recheck treated stands each summer and treat resprouts and suckers.
Triclopyr or glyphosate (cut surface)

schedule.window: Hack-and-squirt, mid to late summer (before fall color): downward cuts spaced around the trunk, about one per inch of diameter, minimum 2

notes: Do not girdle completely. Living tissue between cuts carries herbicide to the roots

treatments.title: Triclopyr or glyphosate (foliar spray)

schedule.window: Low, dense sprouts and seedlings first, then hack-and-squirt larger stems

notes: Keep spray off desirable plants

conditions.name: Jumping worms
biology: Invasive Amynthas earthworms, now widespread in Virginia and Maryland. They turn mulch and topsoil into loose, coffee-ground-like castings, strip organic matter, and leave shallow-rooted plants and new plantings drought-prone. Adults die in winter, and cocoons in the soil carry them to new sites in mulch, compost and plant soil.

treatments.title: Do not move mulch, compost or soil from infested beds. Clean soil off tools and equipment between sites.
Inspect the root balls of incoming plants for worms and castings.
Use fine, well-aged mulch, irrigate new plantings closely, and rebuild organic matter.
